questions.explanation: „Guten Tag“ is the standard daytime greeting. „Guten Morgen“ is used before midday and „Guten Abend“ in the evening — German picks the greeting by the clock more strictly than English does.
„Danke“ is thank you; „bitte“ is please. Confusingly, „bitte“ also means 'you're welcome' — the same word does both jobs, which English keeps separate.
„Bitte“ is please, and also the reply to „danke“. Hearing it after you thank someone is not them saying please — it is 'you're welcome'.
Literally 'until seeing again'. „Tschüss“ is the casual version, used with friends the way 'bye' is in English.
„Das Buch“ is the book, and it is neuter — one of three genders. German capitalises every noun, so „Buch“ keeps its capital anywhere in a sentence.
„Die Schule“ is feminine. There is no way to work that out from the meaning, which is why the article is learned as part of the word.
„Der Bruder“ is masculine; „die Schwester“ is the sister. „Der Vater“ is the father, which is the nearest option and the usual mix-up.
„Das Brot“ is bread. „Das Brötchen“ is a bread roll — the -chen ending makes a small version of something, and always turns the word neuter.
„Das Wasser“ is water. „Das Wetter“ is the weather, which looks close enough to catch people out when reading quickly.
„Rot“ is red. German colour words are not capitalised when used as adjectives, unlike the nouns they describe.
„Blau“ is blue and „schwarz“ is black. The pair is worth learning together because both begin with the same letter in English.

questions.stem: How do you say 'three' in German?
questions.explanation: „Drei“ is three. „Dreizehn“ is thirteen and „dreißig“ is thirty — built from the same root, which is exactly what makes them easy to confuse.

questions.stem: How do you say 'ten' in German?
questions.explanation: „Zehn“ is ten. „Zwei“ (two) and „zwölf“ (twelve) share its opening sound, so the numbers are best drilled as a set.
„Heute“ is today, „gestern“ is yesterday and „morgen“ is tomorrow. Note that „der Morgen“ with a capital is the morning — same word, different job.
„Das Haus“ is neuter. The plural adds an umlaut and -er: „die Häuser“, which is a pattern German uses often.

questions.stem: How do you say 'I am hungry' in German?
questions.explanation: German uses „haben“ for hunger and thirst, like French and unlike English: literally 'I have hunger'. „Ich bin hungrig“ is also correct German, but „ich bin Hunger“ never is.

questions.stem: How do you say 'my name is Alex' in German?
questions.explanation: „Ich heiße“ is the usual way — literally 'I am called'. „Mein Name ist Alex“ is also correct, but the option here mangles it.

questions.stem: What does „Ich bin fünfzehn Jahre alt“ mean?
options: I have been here fifteen years
questions.explanation: Unlike French, German uses „sein“ (to be) for age, exactly as English does. „Jahre alt“ can be dropped in speech, leaving „ich bin fünfzehn“.

questions.stem: How would you ask 'how are you?' politely?
questions.explanation: „Ihnen“ is the formal you. „Dir“ and „wie geht's“ are informal and belong with friends. German draws this line more sharply than English, and using „du“ with a stranger can read as rude.

questions.stem: What does „Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Ich hätte gern“ is the polite way to order — a subjunctive form, softer than „ich will“ ('I want'), which sounds blunt to a German ear.

questions.stem: What does „Wo ist die Toilette?“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Wo“ means where. Note that German uses the singular „die Toilette“ where French insists on the plural.
The most useful sentence a beginner can carry. „Nicht“ goes after the verb, which is where English puts 'not' before it.

questions.stem: How do you say 'the red car' in German?
questions.explanation: The adjective comes before the noun as in English, but it takes an ending that agrees with the noun — „rot“ becomes „rote“. „Auto“ is neuter, so it takes „das“.

questions.stem: What does „Ich habe zwei Schwestern“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Schwestern“ is the plural of „Schwester“. German plurals are irregular enough that each one is worth learning with the word.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I would like a glass of water'?
options: Ich hätte gern einen Glas Wasser
Ich habe gern ein Glas Wasser
Ich hätte gern ein Glas von Wasser
Ich hätte gern ein Glas Wasser
questions.explanation: „Glas“ is neuter, so the accusative article is „ein“ and not „einen“. German does not need 'of' between a container and its contents — „ein Glas Wasser“, never 'ein Glas von Wasser'.

questions.stem: Which correctly says 'it is half past three'?
questions.explanation: This is the trap German learners meet once and never forget: „halb vier“ means half*way to* four, so it is 3:30. „Halb drei“ would be 2:30.

questions.stem: Which sentence means 'there is a book on the table'?
options: Es gibt ein Buch auf dem Tisch
Es ist ein Buch auf dem Tisch
Da hat ein Buch auf dem Tisch
Es gibt ein Buch auf den Tisch
questions.explanation: „Es gibt“ is the fixed expression for 'there is', and it does not change for plural. „Auf dem Tisch“ takes the dative because nothing is moving — „auf den Tisch“ would mean onto the table.
